content:
Yesterday we studied the young bull of the burnt offering the animal of strength, labour, and total surrender, pointing to Christ who bore our burdens with the full vigour of a willing servant and offered Himself wholly to the Father without reservation. Today we move to the second animal of the burnt offering: the ram. Alongside the young bull and the lamb of the first year, each tribal leader brought one ram. Three animals together. Three different messages. And the ram carries one of the most ancient, most personal, and most searching messages of all. The ram is the animal of substitution.

Before we can understand the ram in Numbers 7, we must go back to where the ram first appears as a sacrifice in Scripture. Genesis 22 is one of the most profound and searching accounts in the entire Bible. God commanded Abraham to take his son Isaac; his only son, the son of the promise, the son for whom he had waited a hundred years and offer him as a burnt offering on Mount Moriah. Abraham rose early in the morning, cut the wood, saddled the donkey, and set out with his son. The journey took three days. On the third day Abraham saw the mountain from a distance and left his servants behind. It was father and son alone for the final climb.

Isaac asked the question that must have broken Abraham’s heart: “Behold, the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?” (Genesis 22:7). And Abraham answered with a word that was more prophecy than answer: “God will provide for Himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son” (Genesis 22:8). He bound Isaac. He laid him on the altar. He stretched out his hand and took the knife. And then the angel of Yahweh called from heaven: “Do not lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him, for now I know that you fear God, seeing you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.” And Abraham lifted up his eyes and looked, and behind him was a ram, caught in a thicket by his horns (Genesis 22:13). The ram took Isaac’s place. The ram died so that the son of the promise could live. This is the most explicit picture of substitution in all of Scripture.

Abraham called the name of that place “Yahweh will provide” Yahweh Jireh. And the text adds: “as it is said to this day, on the mount of the LORD it shall be provided” (Genesis 22:14). On that same mountain range; Mount Moriah where Abraham found the ram in the thicket, Solomon would later build the Temple. And near that same mountain, centuries later, the one whom the ram had been pointing to would be crucified. The ram in the thicket was always a promise. The cross was the fulfilment of what Abraham’s knife had begun.

The ram is not a one-time symbol. It appears again and again throughout the Old Testament in the key moments of covenant, consecration, and atonement, building a cumulative portrait that points always in the same direction.
In Exodus 29:15-18, when Aaron and his sons were consecrated for the priesthood, a ram was offered as a burnt offering. The priesthood itself was inaugurated through the blood of a ram. And in Exodus 29:19-20, a second ram the ram of consecration; had its blood applied to the right ear, the right thumb, and the right big toe of Aaron and his sons. The ear that hears. The hand that serves. The foot that walks. Every part of the priest’s ministry was marked and set apart by the blood of the ram.

In Numbers 29, the Day of Atonement offerings included rams. In Ezekiel’s vision of the restored temple, rams appear repeatedly in the dedication offerings of the prince. In Job 42:8, when Yahweh commanded Job’s friends to offer a burnt offering for their wrong words, the offering was seven bulls and seven rams. In each appearance, the ram carries the same character: it is the animal of the significant moment, the animal of covenant consecration, the animal that stands in the place of another when the weight of the requirement is too great for the offerer to bear alone.

And in Isaiah 53:6-7, though the word ram is not used, the portrait of the substitutionary sacrifice reaches its fullest expression: “All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned, every one, to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on Him the iniquity of us all. He was oppressed, and He was afflicted, yet He opened not His mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so He opened not His mouth.” The sheep that have gone astray. The one on whom the iniquity of all was laid. The silent, submitted, not-defending-Himself substitution. This is the ram of Genesis 22 come to its full form.

Now we can see why the ram was included in the burnt offering of Numbers 7 alongside the bull and the lamb. The bull spoke of Christ’s strength and total service. The ram speaks of Christ as the substitute; the one who was found in the thicket so that the condemned could go free. Every element of the Genesis 22 account becomes a key to reading the cross. Isaac carried the wood on his own back up the mountain (Genesis 22:6) as Christ carried His own cross (John 19:17). The father and son walked together for three days and Christ travel with the Father for 3 years since baptism. Isaac was bound and laid on the wood (Genesis 22:9) and Christ was nailed to the wood. And when the knife was raised, Yahweh provided the substitute.

Romans 8:32 makes the connection with breathtaking clarity: “He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all; how will He not also, along with Him, graciously give us all things?” He did not spare. Abraham did not spare Isaac in his heart, and Yahweh provided the ram. The Father did not spare His Son, and the Son became the ram. The language of Genesis 22 and Romans 8 is the same language. The same God. The same Father. The same not-sparing.
The same provision on the mountain.

Galatians 3:13 is the burnt offering ram stated plainly: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us for it is written, cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree.” The ram was caught in the thicket the thorns gripping its horns, unable to move, bound. Christ wore a crown of thorns.
The thorns that held the ram bound were pressed into the brow of the substitute. The ram in the thicket and the one crowned with thorns are the same figure seen from different ends of time.

And 2 Corinthians 5:21 gives us the deepest statement of the substitution: “For our sake He made Him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.” The ram that had done nothing wrong was caught and killed in the place of the one who had been bound for death. Christ who had done nothing wrong was made sin in the place of those who deserved death. The substitution is total, real, and irreversible. Isaac went home from the mountain because the ram did not. We go home to God because Christ stayed on the altar in our place.

This is still the message of the ram for us today. We do not come before God on the basis of our improved behaviour, our religious commitment, or our years of service. We come on the basis of a substitute. 1 Peter 3:18 says: “For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that He might bring us to God.” The righteous for the unrighteous. The ram for Isaac.
The substitute for the condemned. And Hebrews 9:28: “So Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for Him.” Offered once.
The ram was found once in the thicket, and once was enough.
The substitution does not need to be repeated. The thicket held the ram.
The cross held Christ. And both released the one who should have died.

title: Prayer
text:
Yahweh Jireh; You are the God who provides. On the mountain where Abraham raised the knife, You provided the ram. On the mountain where the cross was raised, You provided Your Son. We thank You that we are Isaac that we were bound, that the knife was raised over us, and that at the last moment You provided a substitute. We thank You that Christ wore the thorns that held the ram, that He became the curse so we could receive the blessing, that He stayed on the altar so we could go home. Help us never to treat this substitution as ordinary. Help us never to walk away from the mountain of Moriah as if something small happened there. The ram died. Christ died. Isaac lived.

We live. May the weight of what was given for us shape everything about how we live today. In Christ’s name, amen.
